My projects.

PROJECT 01

Online Retail Sales Analysis

Python, SQL, Pandas, Matplotlib, Plotly

Problem: Find out which products, countries and customers bring the most sales.

  • Analysed 541,909 records and kept 522,502 (96.4%) after cleaning: removed duplicates, cancelled orders, non-product rows and invalid values.
  • Used SQL for monthly sales, top products, countries and returns.
  • Scored 4,333 customers on Recency, Frequency and Monetary value and grouped them into 6 segments using Recency and Frequency (Monetary is shown as spend per segment).
  • Made charts with Matplotlib and Plotly.

Finding 1: Sep–Nov 2011 gave 37.5% of the revenue in the 12 full months, Dec 2010 to Nov 2011 (£3.58M).
Finding 2: Top 20% of customers with an ID bring 74% of the revenue from customers with an ID (£8.49M). Champions are 24% of those customers and 67% of that revenue.
Recommendation: Contact the 384 "At Risk" customers first. They bought often before but stopped.

Data: UCI Online Retail dataset (Dec 2010 to Dec 2011). Notebook, SQL and cleaning log are in the repo.

PROJECT 02

Used Car Price Analysis (India)

Python, Pandas, SQL, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly

Problem: How fast do used cars lose value, and do automatic, diesel and dealer cars really cost more?

  • Analysed 15,411 listings and kept 15,229 after cleaning. Removed 167 duplicates and 15 impossible rows, and fixed brand spelling.
  • Used SQL window functions to compare prices by age, brand and model.

Finding 1: Cars lose about 11% of value per year (4.9% for Maruti Celerio, 16.3% for Mercedes E-Class).
Finding 2: Automatic cars cost 2.1x on raw medians, but only about 1.4x for the same model.
Limit: These are asking prices, not final sale prices.

Data: CarDekho used car listings from Kaggle (asking prices). Notebook, SQL and cleaning log are in the repo.

Data and method: Online Retail
  • Source: UCI Machine Learning Repository, "Online Retail" dataset (link). 541,909 rows, 1 Dec 2010 to 9 Dec 2011 (December 2011 is a part month, marked *). The raw file is 46 MB and is not in the repo.
  • Revenue = Quantity × UnitPrice. Orders = distinct invoice numbers. Customers = distinct customer IDs. Average order value = Revenue ÷ Orders.

Why the chart totals are different (all checked against £10,001,168 total):

  • Monthly revenue adds up to the full £10,001,168.
  • Segments use only the 4,333 customers who have an ID: £8,491,574. The other 131,354 clean rows (25% of rows) have no customer ID and are worth £1,509,593 (15% of revenue). They are shown as "No customer ID", so the pie also adds up to £10,001,168.
  • Countries: the top 6 give £9,561,110; the other 32 countries give £440,057. The chart shows the top 10 and a bar for all the rest, so it adds up to the total.
  • Top 10 products are £819,738, only 8.2% of revenue. Sales are spread over thousands of products. Products are grouped by stock code.

RFM scores and segments: snapshot date = day after the last sale. Recency = days since last order, Frequency = number of orders, Monetary = total spend. Each gets a score from 1 to 5 using percentile cut points (Recency is reversed). The segment rules use only the R and F scores: Champions R≥4 and F≥4; Loyal R≥3 and F≥3; New / Recent R≥4 and F≤2; At Risk R≤2 and F≥3; Lost R≤2 and F≤2; everything else Need Attention. The M score is calculated but is not used in the rules. Monetary is shown as average spend per segment instead (Champions £5,542, Loyal £1,831, At Risk £1,662, Need Attention £521, New £488, Lost £448). I did this because frequency and spend move together in this data (Spearman correlation 0.81). So this is an RF-based segmentation with spend reported, not a three-way RFM rule set.

Check it yourself: the notebook, SQL and data files are in the online-retail-analysis repo. prepare_dashboard_data.py in the portfolio repo builds the 4 .csv files and stops with an error if the totals do not match. Data behind this dashboard (CSV): retail_customer_month.csv, retail_product_month.csv, retail_products.csv.

Make brand spelling consistent (ISUZU and Isuzu)15,41115,4112 changed

Remove cars with 0 seats15,24415,2422

Value lost per year: for each model with at least 100 listings and at least 5 different ages, fit a straight line to log(price) against age. If the slope is s, the loss per year is 100 × (1 − es). The "median across models" is the headline number (about 11% with no filters, 36 models).

for name, s in df.groupby("car_name"):
    if len(s) >= 100 and s["vehicle_age"].nunique() >= 5:
        slope = np.polyfit(s["vehicle_age"], np.log(s["selling_price"]), 1)[0]
        rows.append({"car_name": name, "listings": len(s),
                     "annual_value_loss_pct": 100 * (1 - np.exp(slope))})

Same-model price gap: raw = median price of group A ÷ median price of group B over all cars. Same model = for each model with at least 50 listings in both groups, divide the two medians, then take the median of those ratios. This removes the effect of automatic, diesel or dealer cars simply being different (usually bigger) models.

def same_model_gap(data, col, a, b, min_n=50):
    t = data.groupby(["car_name", col])["selling_price"].agg(["count", "median"]).unstack()
    ok = t[(t[("count", a)] >= min_n) & (t[("count", b)] >= min_n)]
    ratio = ok[("median", a)] / ok[("median", b)]
    return ratio, len(ok)

Limits: asking prices only; 7 cars over ₹1 crore are kept (medians and log scales reduce their effect); 4 rows labelled Electric are really Toyota Camry petrol cars, so fuel comparisons use only Petrol and Diesel. Correlations (engine power 0.72, age −0.48, kilometres −0.17) are in the notebook.

Check it yourself: notebook, SQL (analysis.sql, medians with ROW_NUMBER, LAG, NTILE, RANK) and cleaning log are in the used-car-price-analysis repo. Data behind this dashboard (CSV): cars_cleaned.csv.

Both projects use SQLite. The full files are in the repos: retail analysis.sql (15 queries) and used cars analysis.sql (12 queries). The tables below list what each group of queries answers and which SQL feature it uses.

How I explain it

  • Median without a MEDIAN function: SQLite has none, so I number the rows inside each group with ROW_NUMBER() and take the middle row (or the average of the two middle rows).
  • Why LAG(): to compare each month (or car age) with the one before it, without joining the table to itself.
  • Where I use JOINs: in the used cars file (brand medians joined back to the cars, eligible models joined to their price bands, and a self-join of automatic and manual medians). The retail file works on one cleaned sales table plus a returns table, so it has no JOINs.
  • Same method in SQL and Python: the automatic vs manual query uses medians, like the Python code, so both give 1.42x.

Retail: monthly revenue with LAG()

-- 6. Monthly revenue and change vs previous month
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT month,
           ROUND(SUM(revenue), 0)                                AS revenue,
           COUNT(DISTINCT invoice_no)                            AS orders,
           ROUND(SUM(revenue) / COUNT(DISTINCT invoice_no), 2)   AS avg_order_value
    FROM sales
    GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, revenue, orders, avg_order_value,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1)            AS pct_change_vs_prev_month
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

Used cars: same-model automatic vs manual (medians)

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT car_name, transmission_type, selling_price,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY car_name, transmission_type ORDER BY selling_price) AS rn,
           COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY car_name, transmission_type)                        AS n
    FROM cars
    WHERE transmission_type IN ('Automatic', 'Manual')
),
m AS (   -- median price of each model for each transmission (models need 50+ listings per transmission)
    SELECT car_name, transmission_type, MAX(n) AS n, AVG(selling_price) AS median_price
    FROM ranked
    WHERE n >= 50 AND rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2)
    GROUP BY car_name, transmission_type
)
SELECT a.car_name, a.n AS automatic_listings, b.n AS manual_listings,
       ROUND(a.median_price, 0) AS automatic_median, ROUND(b.median_price, 0) AS manual_median,
       ROUND(a.median_price / b.median_price, 2) AS automatic_vs_manual
FROM m a JOIN m b ON a.car_name = b.car_name
WHERE a.transmission_type = 'Automatic' AND b.transmission_type = 'Manual'
ORDER BY automatic_vs_manual DESC;
